segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Let brotherly love remain.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do not forget hospitality to strangers, for through it some have hosted angels without knowing it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Remember the prisoners as though imprisoned with them, and those who are mistreated, since you yourselves are also in a body.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Let marriage be held in honor by all, and let the marriage bed be undefiled, for God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterers.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Keep your way of life free from the love of money, and be content with what you have, for he himself has said,

segments.speaker: God
segments.text: “I will never leave you, and I will never abandon you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So we can say with confidence,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “The Lord is my helper; I will not be afraid. What can a human being do to me?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Remember your leaders, who spoke the word of God to you. Consider the outcome of their conduct, and imitate their faith.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today, and forever.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do not be carried away by all kinds of strange teachings, for it is good for the heart to be made firm by grace, not by foods, which have not benefited those who live by them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: We have an altar from which those who serve the tent have no right to eat.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the bodies of the animals whose blood is brought into the holy place by the high priest as an offering for sin are burned outside the camp.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So Jesus also suffered outside the gate, in order to make the people holy through his own blood.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, let us go out to him outside the camp, bearing the abuse he bore.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For here we have no city that remains, but we are seeking the one that is to come.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Through him, then, let us continually offer up to God a sacrifice of praise, that is, the fruit of lips that acknowledge his name.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And do not forget to do good and to share, for with such sacrifices God is pleased.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Obey your leaders and yield to them, for they keep watch over your souls as those who will give an account, so that they may do this with joy and not with groaning, for that would be of no advantage to you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Pray for us, for we are convinced that we have a good conscience, wanting to conduct ourselves well in everything.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I exhort you all the more to do this, so that I may be restored to you sooner.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now may the God of peace, who brought up from the dead the great shepherd of the sheep by the blood of an eternal covenant, our Lord Jesus,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: equip you with every good thing to do his will, working in us what is pleasing in his sight through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever. Amen.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I exhort you, brothers and sisters, bear with this word of exhortation, for I have written to you only briefly.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Know that our brother Timothy has been released. If he comes soon, I will see you with him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Greet all your leaders and all the holy ones. Those from Italy greet you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Grace be with you all.

notes.note: The allusion is to Abraham and Lot, who welcomed travellers who turned out to be divine messengers (Genesis 18–19). The Greek plays on two related verbs, “forget” and “escape notice”, and pairs “love of brothers” (v. 1) with “love of strangers” (hospitality).

notes.phrase: Let marriage be held in honor by all
notes.note: The Greek has no verb. Most modern translations supply a command, as here, because the surrounding sentences are exhortations; older versions read it as a statement (“marriage is honourable”). The phrase rendered “by all” could also mean “in every respect”.

What teaching about food is meant is disputed. Most scholars think of Jewish food regulations or sacred meals linked to sacrifice, in line with the letter's earlier remark about rules of food and drink (9:10); the argument in verses 10–12 moves straight to the altar and its offerings.

The Greek word is the ordinary one for a tent and here means the tent-sanctuary Israel carried in the wilderness. “Tabernacle” is the traditional English term, and several modern translations already use “tent”. Hebrews argues from the wilderness tent as described in the Law throughout, not from the Jerusalem temple.

On the Day of Atonement the high priest carried the blood of the sin offerings into the inner sanctuary, and the carcasses were not eaten but burned outside Israel's camp (Leviticus 16:27). The author sees this matched in Jesus' execution outside the city gate (v. 12). “As an offering for sin” renders the Septuagint's set phrase for the sin offering, literally “concerning sin”.

notes.traditional: giving thanks to his name; confess his name
notes.note: The verb normally means to declare or acknowledge openly. With “to his name” it may instead echo the Septuagint idiom for praising or giving thanks to God's name, which would suit “sacrifice of praise”. “Fruit of lips” is itself a Septuagint phrase (Hosea 14:2).

The verb's basic sense is “be persuaded”. With a person as its object it regularly meant to comply with or obey them, and the traditional rendering is kept. Some interpreters prefer “trust” or “be persuaded by”, stressing willing assent. The same verb appears in verse 18 as “we are convinced”.
Manuscripts are divided between “in us” and “in you”; the two Greek pronouns differ by one letter and were pronounced alike. The SBLGNT reads “us”, which is followed here.

The plural was the normal way to address a mixed group of men and women as siblings, and the letter is written to the whole community. Many modern translations render it this way, while others keep “brothers”. The same root lies behind “brotherly love” in verse 1.

The same phrase is used in Acts 13:15 for an address given in the synagogue after the Scripture readings, so the author is probably describing the whole work as a sermon sent in writing. The noun covers both urging and encouragement, and the verb “I exhort” is from the same root.

Most take this to mean release from custody, though no imprisonment of Timothy is recorded elsewhere. The verb can also mean “sent off” or “departed”, so it may only say that he has set out. “Know” could also be read as a statement: “you know”.

“Saints” now suggests canonised individuals or people of unusual virtue. The word is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint's language for Israel. Many translations keep “saints”, and others use “God's people”.

The phrase can mean people who are in Italy, which would make Italy the place of writing, or Italians living elsewhere who send greetings home, which would make Italy the destination. The Greek does not settle it, and scholars are divided.

candidates.reason: The plural address to mixed communities recurs throughout the letters, and translators split between “brothers” and “brothers and sisters”; it also bears on compounds like φιλαδελφία.
It ranges over “life”, “self” and “soul” across the New Testament, and “soul” often imports a later body–soul dualism, so a governing policy is needed.
It is central in Hebrews, Paul and the Last Supper accounts, and it shifts between “covenant” and “will/testament” (Hebrews 9:16–17; Galatians 3:15).
“Sanctify” is opaque to modern readers and hides the link with ἅγιος, so it should be decided once alongside the “holy ones” entry.
It is very frequent, and translators vary between urge, appeal, exhort, encourage and comfort; the verb–noun wordplay with παράκλησις needs a consistent policy.
